subject: PO: Dedicated GPU sizing for ArdentTX – context headroom + quant tradeoffs
messages:
From: Dr. Lena Morales <lena.morales@ardenttx.com>
To: Olga Petrov <olga_petrov@redwood.ai>
Cc: Roberto Diaz <rdiaz@ardenttx.com>
Date: Sat, 1 May 2027 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Dedicated pool sizing request — long-context clinical QA model

Hi Olga,

Thanks again for the demo yesterday. Our teams are excited to move forward with a dedicated pool for the clinical question-answering pipeline. A couple of clarifying bullets for the PO:
- Model: open-variant we evaluated (LlamaX-30B-like) with 65k context in production.
- Peak concurrent requests: ~80 qps for short queries, spikes to 200 qps during nightly reprocessing.
- Average prompt length: 1.2k tokens; tail requests up to 60k tokens (we'll rely on retrieval but still see long contexts).
- Latency SLO: 300ms p50 for short queries; best-effort for long tail.
- Current ask: a committed monthly pool with headroom for feature rollout through Q3.

What we need from Redwood: a recommended pod count and GPU class, and an assessment of how much memory we can save by switching to 4-bit quantization vs FP16 + any caveats for KV cache behavior with 60k windows.

Appreciate a quick runbook and any attachment you can include for procurement. We need the PO by end of week.

Best,
Lena
VP AI Engineering
Ardent Therapeutics

From: Olga Petrov <olga_petrov@redwood.ai>
To: Dr. Lena Morales <lena.morales@ardenttx.com>
Cc: Sean Gallagher <sean_gallagher@redwood.ai>
Date: Mon, 3 May 2027 08:47:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Dedicated pool sizing request — long-context clinical QA model

Lena — thanks for the clear asks. Looping in Sean (sales) and Marcus (runtime) to produce an ops-ready sizing & procurement sheet.

Quick notes while we pull numbers:
- Long contexts dominate memory because KV caches scale linearly with sequence length. For a 30B-style architecture, native KV in FP16 is expensive.
- Quantization (4-bit) reduces model weights footprint substantially, but KV cache math is nuanced: KV storage is dominated by activations/keys/values which can also be quantized or offloaded depending on runtime.

Action plan: Marcus will run two scenarios (FP16 baseline and 4-bit weights + 8-bit KV) across your workload profile and produce recommended reserved pod counts and preferred GPU class (A100 80GB vs H100 80GB). Sean will prepare contract language for a monthly pool with burst credits.

I'll attach a short capacity worksheet for procurement next message. If procurement needs a PO template, mention it now and we'll include.

Thanks,
Olga
Senior Solutions Engineer
Redwood Inference

Olga Petrov
Redwood Inference

From: Marcus Lin <marcus_lin@redwood.ai>
To: Olga Petrov <olga_petrov@redwood.ai>, Sean Gallagher <sean_gallagher@redwood.ai>, Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.ai>
Date: Wed, 5 May 2027 10:06:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Dedicated pool sizing request — long-context clinical QA model

Folks — attached is the scenario workbook (ardent_kv_capacity_sheet.xlsx) and an explainer PDF (quant-impact-scenarios.pdf). Executive summary below; details are in the attachments.

Executive summary (numbers are rounded and include 20% operational headroom):
- Baseline (FP16 weights, FP16 KV):
  - Effective GPU memory required per concurrent long-request worker: ~62 GB (model + KV with 60k window, 1.2k avg prompt case is much lower).
  - Pod recommendation (reserved, 1:1 worker per GPU for latency-sensitive): 10 pods of A100-80GB to cover steady qps with burst to 200 qps using autoscaling buffer.

- Optimized (4-bit weight quantization, 8-bit KV, runtime KV compression + selective offload):
  - Effective GPU memory per worker: ~38–42 GB (weights compressed; KV reduced via 2x compression + 8-bit store; selective prefix offload for >16k tokens).
  - Pod recommendation: 6–7 pods of H100-80GB (H100 preferred for faster batch throughput and better mixed-precision kernels).

Notes and tradeoffs:
- Quantization savings: weight size drops ~45–55% moving to a calibrated 4-bit scheme. However real-world memory saved depends on whether KV is stored in compressed form on-GPU or offloaded to NVMe/DRAM.
- Long tail requests (30k–60k tokens): even with aggressive quant and compression, we recommend a hybrid strategy:
  1) Keep a small pool of "long-runner" GPUs with increased KV offload tolerance (we measured ~20% slower latency for offloaded segments).
  2) Configure prefix caching for repeated document contexts to avoid re-populating full KV for common retrievals.
- Headroom and burst: to meet 200 qps spikes, we model a burst buffer of 40% on top of steady state. For strict latency SLOs, prefer 1:1 worker-to-GPU for short queries. For throughput-first pipelines, we can multiplex multiple workers with batching.
- Cost/ops: H100 pods (with optimized quant) reduce unit-hour token cost by ~28% vs A100 FP16 baseline given your mix of long- and short-context traffic.

I've included a sample GPU assignment table in the workbook mapping expected concurrency bands -> reserved pods. Kimberly — please add a short bullet in the workbook about runtime knob recommendations (KV compression flags, max_offload_segment_size, prefix_cache_ttl).

Marcus Lin
Principal Infrastructure Engineer, Redwood Inference

Attachments: ardent_kv_capacity_sheet.xlsx (pod mapping & numbers), quant-impact-scenarios.pdf (benchmarks and latency/cost curves)
